essays.stem: A salon owner in Ocho Rios wants to know if clients would pay for a new natural-hair care service. Describe how you would plan this research.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would write a clear aim, such as 'To find out if clients would use and pay for a natural-hair care service.' Then I would list objectives: how many clients have natural hair, which services they want, how often they would come, and what price they would pay. Next I would choose methods. For primary data, I could give a short questionnaire to clients over two weeks and interview a few stylists. For secondary data, I could look at the price lists and websites of other salons and any trade reports on hair trends. I would decide on the sample, such as 50 clients across different days and times, so the results are fair. I would plan the timeline, with a date for each step and a deadline for the report, and a budget for printing and any small gifts. I would also plan how to get consent and keep answers private, and test the questionnaire on a few people first.
markingPoints: Writes a clear aim and specific objectives
Chooses suitable primary methods (questionnaire, interviews)
Chooses suitable secondary sources (competitors, trade reports)
Plans a fair sample, a timeline with a deadline, and a budget
Plans consent and privacy, and pilots the questionnaire

essays.stem: Compare primary and secondary research. Give one salon example of each, and one strength and one weakness of each.
essays.modelAnswer: Primary research means collecting new information yourself for your own purpose. A salon example is giving a questionnaire to clients about the opening hours they want. Its strength is that it is up to date and about your own salon and clients, so it answers your exact question. Its weakness is that it takes time and costs money to plan, collect and count. Secondary research means using information that someone else has already collected, such as a government report on household spending, a trade magazine article on beauty trends, or other salons' price lists. Its strength is that it is often quick and cheap to get, and it can cover a large area, such as the whole of Jamaica. Its weakness is that it may be out of date, may not be about your type of salon or clients, and may be biased, so it must be checked. Many researchers start with secondary research and then use primary research to fill the gaps.
markingPoints: Defines primary research and gives a salon example
Gives a strength and a weakness of primary research
Defines secondary research and gives a salon example
Gives a strength and a weakness of secondary research
Compares them or says how they can be used together

essays.stem: Describe how to design a good client questionnaire, and explain what to avoid.
essays.modelAnswer: I would start with the aim, so that every question helps answer it, and keep the questionnaire short, about 8 to 10 questions, so clients finish it. At the top I explain what it is for, how long it takes, that taking part is their choice, and that answers are private. I use simple, clear words and one idea per question. Most questions should be closed, with tick boxes or a rating scale from 1 to 5, because they are quick to answer and easy to count. I add one or two open questions for comments. The questions go in a sensible order, starting with easy ones. I avoid leading questions, such as 'Don't you love our new prices?', and questions that ask two things at once. I avoid trade jargon and personal questions that are not needed, such as income or address. Before using it, I test it on a few people and fix anything that confuses them. Finally, I thank people at the end.
markingPoints: Links every question to the aim; short length
Introduction explains the purpose, choice and privacy
Simple wording; mostly closed or rating questions, plus a few open questions
Avoids leading, double, jargon and unnecessary personal questions
Tests the questionnaire first and fixes problems

essays.stem: Explain how to judge whether a source of information is reliable, using the example of information found online about a new hair product.
essays.modelAnswer: First I look at who wrote it. Information from the maker's official site, a health authority or a known trade body is more reliable than an unnamed post. Then I ask why it was written. If it is an advert or a paid post, it is trying to sell the product, so it may only show the good side. Next I check the date, because product information and prices change, and old information may be wrong now. I look for facts that can be checked, such as the ingredient list or results of tests, rather than only opinions like 'this is the best product ever'. I compare it with other sources, such as a trade magazine, the product label and the safety data sheet, to see if they agree. I also check whether the information is about Jamaica or our climate and hair types. If several reliable sources agree, I can trust it more. I write down each source so it can be checked again.
markingPoints: Checks the author or owner of the source
Checks the purpose and possible bias (adverts, paid posts)
Checks the date
Looks for facts rather than opinions, and compares with other sources
Checks that it fits the local situation and records the sources

essays.stem: Explain the ethical rules a researcher must follow when collecting information from clients.
essays.modelAnswer: Ethics means doing research in an honest and fair way that respects people. First, people must give consent. The researcher explains what the research is for, how the information will be used and how long it takes, and makes clear that taking part is a free choice. Nobody should be pressured, for example by saying they will lose their booking. Second, privacy must be protected. The researcher only asks for personal details that are really needed, does not put names on answers where possible, and keeps forms and computer files locked away or protected by a password. Information is only used for the stated purpose and is not shared or sold. Third, the researcher must be honest. Results are reported exactly as they were found, even if the owner does not like them, and numbers are never changed or made up. Finally, people are treated with respect: questions are polite, and a person may stop at any time.
markingPoints: Gets informed consent; taking part is a free choice, with no pressure
Asks only for details that are needed and keeps answers anonymous where possible
Stores data securely and uses it only for the stated purpose
Reports results honestly, with no changed or made-up figures
Treats people with respect and lets them stop at any time

essays.stem: Explain why the choice of people to survey matters, and how a salon can avoid bias in its sample.
essays.modelAnswer: The sample is the group of people who take part in the research. If the sample does not represent the whole group the salon cares about, the results can be wrong. For example, if the owner only asks her friends, they may say what she wants to hear. If she only asks Saturday morning clients, she will miss the views of workers who come in the evenings or older clients who come midweek. This is called bias. To avoid it, the salon should choose a sample that is large enough, for example at least 30 to 50 clients, and mixed. The survey should be given on different days and at different times, to clients of different ages, to both men and women, and for different services. The staff should offer it to every client, or every second client, instead of choosing only the ones they like. Questions should not be leading, and staff should not stand over people while they answer.
markingPoints: Explains what a sample is
Explains that an unrepresentative sample gives wrong or biased results, with an example
Uses a large enough sample
Mixes days, times, ages and services, and selects fairly (everyone, or every second client)
Avoids leading questions and pressure while answering

essays.stem: Describe how you would record and organise the answers from 40 completed questionnaires so that they can be analysed.
essays.modelAnswer: First I would number each questionnaire from 1 to 40, so I can find any form again and none are counted twice. I would check every form for missing or unclear answers and decide how to treat them, for example as 'no answer'. Then I would set up a table or spreadsheet, with one row for each questionnaire and one column for each question. For closed questions, I would enter the ticked answer or the rating score. For open questions, I would type the comments and then group similar ones under headings, such as 'prices' or 'waiting time'. I could also make a tally chart on paper first for each closed question, then enter the totals. After entering the data, I would check it against the forms, perhaps with a partner reading them out. I would save the spreadsheet with a clear name and keep a backup. The paper forms would be stored safely in a labelled folder to keep clients' answers private.
markingPoints: Numbers the forms and checks them for missing answers
Sets up a table or spreadsheet with rows for forms and columns for questions
Enters closed answers and groups open comments under headings (tally if useful)
Checks the entered data against the forms
Saves, backs up and stores the forms securely

essays.stem: A survey of 40 clients found that 22 want Sunday opening, 12 want late evenings and 6 want no change. Work out each percentage, explain what the results show, and say what you would recommend.
essays.modelAnswer: To find each percentage, I divide the number by 40 and multiply by 100. Sunday opening is 22 divided by 40, which is 0.55, so 55%. Late evenings is 12 divided by 40, which is 0.3, so 30%. No change is 6 divided by 40, which is 0.15, so 15%. The three add up to 100%, which checks my working. The results show that most clients, 85%, want some change to the opening hours, and the largest group, just over half, want Sunday opening. Late evenings are less popular but still wanted by almost a third. Only a small group is happy as things are. I would recommend that the salon tries Sunday opening for a trial period, such as two months, and keeps records of bookings to see if it pays. Before deciding, the owner should check staff availability and costs. The salon could also try one late evening a week. The sample is only 40 clients, so the results should be checked over time.
markingPoints: Shows the method: divide by 40, multiply by 100
Correct answers: 55%, 30% and 15%, with a check that they total 100%
Explains what the results show (most want change; Sunday is most popular)
Makes a sensible recommendation, such as a trial of Sunday opening with records kept
Notes limits, such as staff, costs or the small sample

essays.stem: Explain how to choose the right chart to present findings, comparing bar charts, pie charts and line graphs.
essays.modelAnswer: The right chart depends on what the data shows. A bar chart uses bars of different heights to compare amounts in different groups, such as the number of clients for hair, nails and skin services, or prices at five local salons. It is easy to read and good for comparing. A pie chart is a circle cut into slices, and each slice shows a share of a whole. It is good for showing what part of total sales came from each service, but only works when the parts add up to 100% and there are not too many slices. A line graph joins points with a line and is best for showing change over time, such as monthly sales over a year, because the trend up or down is easy to see. Whatever chart I use, I give it a clear title, label both axes or every slice, show the units, such as J$ or number of clients, and use a key if needed.
markingPoints: Bar chart: compares amounts between groups, with an example
Pie chart: shows shares of a whole that add up to 100%, with an example
Line graph: shows change over time or trends, with an example
Explains that the choice depends on what the data shows
Every chart needs a title, labels, units and a key where needed

essays.stem: Describe what a short research report to a salon owner should contain, and how the findings and recommendations should be presented.
essays.modelAnswer: A short report starts with a title, the date and the writer's name, then a brief summary of the main findings and recommendations, so a busy owner can read it quickly. Next comes the aim, saying what the research set out to find out. The method section explains how the information was collected, such as a questionnaire given to 50 clients over two weeks, plus the price lists of five other salons. The findings section gives the results in plain words, with simple tables or charts, and percentages or averages where useful. Findings must be honest, including results the owner may not like. Then the conclusions explain what the findings mean for the salon. The recommendations are clear, practical actions based on the findings, such as 'Try Sunday opening for two months', each with a reason. Finally, there is a list of sources. The report should be short, neat and well set out, with headings, and free of jargon.
markingPoints: Title and summary at the start
Aim and method
Findings presented honestly, with tables or charts
Conclusions and practical recommendations, each with a reason
List of sources; clear headings and plain, neat layout

practical1.title: Plan and carry out a client-needs survey at the Centre
practical1.brief: As a group, plan and carry out a short survey on what people want from a local salon or spa (for example opening hours, new services such as natural-hair care or men's grooming, and prices). In stages: (1) write the aim and three objectives on a research plan sheet, with the sample, the timeline and any costs; (2) each member writes two questions, then the group chooses 8 to 10 questions, mostly closed or rating questions with one open question, and adds a short introduction that explains the purpose, says taking part is a free choice and that no names are needed; (3) test the questionnaire on two people, mark the changes and make a final copy; (4) each member collects answers from at least four people at the Centre (trainees or staff who agree), so the group has at least 20; (5) number the forms, check them, and make a tally chart on chart paper for each closed question; (6) enter the totals into a spreadsheet on a Centre computer. Do not collect names, phone numbers or addresses. Survey only inside the Centre and only people who agree. Photograph each stage and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Paper, pens, clipboards and access to a printer or photocopier
Chart paper, markers and a ruler for tally charts
A Centre computer with a spreadsheet program
A labelled folder for the completed forms
A phone or camera for photos
photos: The draft questionnaire with the test changes marked
The final questionnaire with its introduction
The numbered, completed forms in the folder (no personal details visible)
The tally charts for the closed questions
The spreadsheet on screen, with the totals entered
checklist: Helped write a clear aim and objectives linked to the survey
Wrote two clear, simple questions that are not leading
Helped test the questionnaire and make sensible changes
Explained the purpose and asked for consent before each person answered
Collected answers from at least four people politely and without pressure
Tallied answers accurately and checked them with a partner
Entered data into the spreadsheet correctly
Kept completed forms private and stored them in the folder
safety: Survey only inside the Centre, in safe areas, not in the car park or on the road
Ask only people who agree, and accept 'no' politely
Do not collect names, phone numbers or addresses; keep the forms in the folder
At the computer, sit with good posture, keep cables tidy and take short breaks

practical2.title: Analyse price and sales data and present a short report
practical2.brief: As a group, analyse a data pack and present your findings to the salon owner, played by the assessor. The pack (made up for practice) holds price lists from five salons and spas in one Jamaican town, a table of one salon's monthly sales for six months by service (hair, nails, skin and retail), and a short supplier leaflet about a new product. In stages: (1) check each source: who wrote it, the date, and whether it may be biased, and note this on a source sheet; (2) build a comparison table of the prices for four common services and work out the average price of each; (3) work out each service's share of the six months' total sales as a percentage; (4) draw a bar chart comparing prices and a line graph of monthly sales, by hand on graph paper or on a Centre computer, with titles, labels and units; (5) write a one-page report with a summary, aim, method, findings, and two or three recommendations with reasons; (6) present the report, with each member explaining one part and answering questions. Give each member a lead part, such as the source check, the table, the calculations, a chart, the report or the presentation, and check each other's work. Photograph each stage and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: A data pack from the assessor (price lists, sales table and supplier leaflet)
Graph paper, rulers, pencils and coloured pencils
A Centre computer with a spreadsheet and word processor (optional)
A phone or camera for photos
photos: The price comparison table with the averages
The percentage working for each service's share of sales
The finished bar chart of prices
The finished line graph of monthly sales
The presentation to the owner (papers and charts only)
checklist: Judged the reliability of the sources sensibly and noted any bias
Entered the figures in the table accurately
Calculated averages and percentages correctly and checked them
Drew a suitable chart with a title, labels and units
Wrote findings honestly, based only on the data
Made practical recommendations that follow from the findings
Explained their part clearly and answered questions
Checked another member's work and worked well with the group
safety: At the computer, sit with good posture, keep cables tidy and take short breaks
Keep the work area tidy, with bags and chairs out of the walkways
Use only the made-up data in the pack; do not use real clients' details
Use rulers and any paper cutter carefully
